dispatch

/dih-SPATCH/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Dispatch means to send off a person, group, or message to carry out a duty or reach a destination.

When the restaurant's walk-in freezer failed on a Saturday night, the repair company agreed to dispatch a technician within the hour.

Example

The moment the story broke overseas, the newspaper's editor chose to dispatch her most experienced reporter to cover it firsthand.

The editor officially sent the reporter off with a specific job to do. Dispatch is stronger than plain 'send' — it suggests an official order carried out promptly and for a purpose.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

deploy: Deploy means to send people or equipment into position for action — a general deploys troops along a border, a city deploys plows before a storm. Dispatch is the act of sending someone off promptly on a specific errand or duty. You deploy forces across a zone; you dispatch one courier to one address.

forward: Forward means to send a message or package onward to a further address — something that has already arrived once gets passed along. Dispatch starts the journey: headquarters dispatches a courier; an assistant forwards an email. If the thing is being passed along rather than sent out fresh, forward is the word.

transmit: Transmit means to send signals, data, or messages from one point to another over a channel — radios transmit, satellites transmit. Dispatch sends people and vehicles off on duties. You transmit the coordinates; you dispatch the rescue team that drives to them.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

recall: to call someone back

withhold: to hold back and not send

Where it sits · how much urgency is attached

send → dispatch → rush

send vs. dispatch: Send is the neutral, everyday word for making something go somewhere, with no urgency attached; dispatch is stronger, sending someone off briskly and on purpose to carry out a duty.

rush vs. dispatch: Rush carries even more urgency than dispatch, hinting that speed matters more than anything else.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-: away, apart (Latin)

Root — -patch: from Italian dispacciare / Spanish despachar, 'to send off quickly, free from hindrance' — this piece survives only in this word and is not a reusable English root

Put it together: The dis- ('away') is genuine Latin, but the rest of the word came into English whole from Italian dispacciare, 'to send off quickly' — the '-patch' piece never became a reusable English root, so no root drill this time.

Use the root in a new word: dispatcher: The taxi dispatcher spent all night on the radio, sending drivers wherever riders were waiting.

Word Building

Word Choice

official / business

Dispatch is the word of headquarters and control rooms — companies, stations, and agencies dispatch people and vehicles. It also lives as a noun (a reporter's dispatch from abroad; doing something 'with dispatch' means doing it fast), and in older writing it can euphemistically mean 'to kill swiftly' — this card teaches the send-off verb.
